flashcards.question: What is the difference between TRAVEL and TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
TRAVEL = the activity of travellers; a TRAVELLER is anyone moving between geographic locations for ANY purpose and ANY duration.

TOURISM = the activity of VISITORS. Tourism is therefore a SUBSET of travel, and visitors are a subset of travellers.
flashcards.explanation: Key framing from the UN International Recommendations for Tourism Statistics (2008).

flashcards.question: What is a VISITOR, and how is a TOURIST different from an EXCURSIONIST?
flashcards.answer:
A VISITOR is a traveller taking a trip to a main destination OUTSIDE their usual environment, for LESS THAN A YEAR, for any purpose other than being employed by a resident entity there.

• TOURIST (overnight visitor) = the trip INCLUDES an overnight stay
• SAME-DAY VISITOR / EXCURSIONIST = no overnight stay
flashcards.explanation: Overnight stay is the dividing line between tourist and excursionist.

flashcards.question: What are the 3 BASIC FORMS of tourism (by country of reference)?
flashcards.answer:
1. DOMESTIC tourism — resident visitor WITHIN the country of reference
2. INBOUND tourism — NON-resident visitor within the country of reference
3. OUTBOUND tourism — resident visitor OUTSIDE the country of reference
flashcards.explanation: Defined relative to the 'country of reference'.

flashcards.question: How do the 3 basic forms combine into INTERNAL, NATIONAL and INTERNATIONAL tourism?
flashcards.answer:
• INTERNAL = DOMESTIC + INBOUND (all activity within the country)
• NATIONAL = DOMESTIC + OUTBOUND (all activity of residents)
• INTERNATIONAL = INBOUND + OUTBOUND (all cross-border activity)
flashcards.explanation: Three derived forms built from the three basic ones.

flashcards.question: What is a TOURISM DESTINATION (UN Tourism)?
flashcards.answer:
A PHYSICAL SPACE (with or without administrative boundaries) in which a visitor can spend an OVERNIGHT.

It is the cluster (co-location) of products, services, activities and experiences along the tourism value chain, and the basic unit of analysis of tourism. It is also intangible — its IMAGE and IDENTITY influence its market competitiveness.
flashcards.explanation: A destination can be a country, region, island, town or a self-contained centre.

flashcards.question: What is SUSTAINABLE TOURISM?
flashcards.answer: "Tourism that takes full account of its current and future ECONOMIC, SOCIAL and ENVIRONMENTAL impacts, addressing the needs of visitors, the industry, the environment and host communities" (UNWTO, 2005).
flashcards.explanation: The three pillars: economic, social, environmental.

flashcards.question: What is a TOURISM PRODUCT?
flashcards.answer:
A combination of TANGIBLE and INTANGIBLE elements — natural, cultural and man-made resources, attractions, facilities, services and activities — around a specific centre of interest.

It is the core of the destination marketing mix, creates an overall visitor experience, is priced and sold through distribution channels, and has a LIFE-CYCLE.
flashcards.explanation: Tangible + intangible around a 'centre of interest'.

flashcards.question: How many SDGs are there, and how does tourism relate to them?
flashcards.answer:
There are 17 interrelated Sustainable Development Goals (169 targets, 231 indicators).

The 'SDGs Wedding Cake' shows three pillars: ENVIRONMENT (biosphere) as the base, SOCIETY as the middle layer, ECONOMY at the top. Well-managed tourism can advance all 17 SDGs when sustainability is a shared responsibility.
flashcards.explanation: 17 SDGs; tourism cuts across the environment–society–economy pillars.

flashcards.question: What is the TOURISM VALUE CHAIN?
flashcards.answer:
The sequence of PRIMARY and SUPPORT activities strategically fundamental to the tourism sector's performance.

• PRIMARY: policy & planning, product development & packaging, promotion & marketing, distribution & sales, destination operations & services
• SUPPORT: transport & infrastructure, HR development, technology & systems, complementary goods/services
flashcards.explanation: Used to trace income flow and find collaborative value.

learn.title: Introduction to Tourism and Sustainability
learn.content:
Key Definitions (UN, 2010)

TRAVEL = activity of travellers (any purpose, any duration)
TOURISM = activity of VISITORS → a subset of travel
TOURIST = overnight visitor · EXCURSIONIST = same-day visitor

Forms of Tourism

  • Basic: Domestic · Inbound · Outbound
  • Derived: Internal (D+I) · National (D+O) · International (I+O)

Destination & Product

A tourism destination is a physical space where a visitor can spend an overnight — a cluster of products and experiences whose image/identity drives competitiveness. A tourism product combines tangible + intangible elements and has a life-cycle.

Sustainability & SDGs

Sustainable tourism balances economic, social and environmental impacts. The 17 SDGs ('Wedding Cake': environment → society → economy) can all be advanced by well-managed tourism.

Tourism Value Chain

Primary activities (policy, product, marketing, distribution, operations) + support activities (transport, HR, technology) — used to trace income and create collaborative value.

flashcards.question: What are the 6 ELEMENTS of a tourism destination (WTO, 2007)?
flashcards.answer:
1. ATTRACTIONS (natural or cultural; the main pull motive)
2. PUBLIC & PRIVATE AMENITIES (infrastructure + private providers)
3. ACCESSIBILITY (how tourists reach and move around)
4. HUMAN RESOURCES (trained staff + welcoming local community)
5. IMAGE & CHARACTER (awareness + matching expectations)
6. PRICE (costs, exchange rates, profit to reinvest)
flashcards.explanation: Sometimes remembered as the 6 A's: Attractions, Amenities, Access, ... + HR, Image, Price.

flashcards.question: What is DESTINATION MANAGEMENT (WTO, 2007)?
flashcards.answer:
The COORDINATED management of all the elements that make up a destination (attractions, amenities, access, marketing, HR, pricing).

It takes a STRATEGIC approach to link separate entities, avoids duplication (promotion, visitor services, training) and identifies management gaps.
flashcards.explanation: 'Joined-up' coordinated management of all destination elements.

flashcards.question: What is a DMO?
flashcards.answer:
A DESTINATION MANAGEMENT ORGANISATION — the 'manager' of the destination.

It plans the development of the destination, promotes it, and acts as the 'GLUE' between all stakeholders. It uses STRATEGIC PLANNING (long-term planning toward strategic goals, a united vision, consistency of action, quality).
flashcards.explanation: Considers how ENDS (goals) are achieved by MEANS (resources) in a given time.

flashcards.question: What are the 4 STEPS of strategic planning in a destination?
flashcards.answer:
1. SITUATION ANALYSIS — assessing the destination's competitiveness
2. STRATEGIC FRAMEWORK — vision, goals, objectives, core strategies
3. IMPLEMENTATION — turning visions/goals into actions
4. MEASURING effects and performance
flashcards.explanation: Analyse → frame → implement → measure.

flashcards.question: What are the key TASKS of a DMO?
flashcards.answer:
a) Destination PLANNING & development (infrastructure, zoning, environment, product)
b) MARKETING & branding (digital/social, events, partnerships, targeted ads)
c) STAKEHOLDER collaboration & governance
d) SUSTAINABLE tourism practices
e) CRISIS & risk management
flashcards.explanation: Five core task areas of destination management.

flashcards.question: What are the main CHALLENGES in destination management?
flashcards.answer:
• OVERTOURISM — overcrowding, environmental degradation, resident dissatisfaction
• ENVIRONMENTAL concerns — pollution, deforestation, habitat loss
• ECONOMIC DEPENDENCE on tourism — vulnerability to external shocks (need diversification)
• POLITICAL & SOCIAL instability — unrest, terrorism, health crises (e.g. COVID-19)
flashcards.explanation: Four recurring challenges.

flashcards.question: What are the future TRENDS in destination management?
flashcards.answer:
• SMART destinations & digital innovation (big data, AI, AR/VR, contactless)
• REGENERATIVE tourism (leave the destination better than before)
• INCLUSIVE & accessible tourism
• LOCAL & SLOW tourism (quality over quantity, authentic immersive experiences)
flashcards.explanation: Smart, regenerative, inclusive, slow.

learn.title: Destination Management
learn.content:
What Makes a Destination?

6 elements (WTO 2007): Attractions · Amenities (public & private) · Accessibility · Human Resources · Image & Character · Price

Destination Management & the DMO

Coordinated management of all destination elements, taking a strategic approach. The DMO plans, promotes and links stakeholders — the 'glue'.

4 Steps of Strategic Planning

1. Situation analysis → 2. Strategic framework (vision/goals) → 3. Implementation → 4. Measuring performance

DMO Tasks

  • Planning & development · Marketing & branding · Stakeholder governance
  • Sustainable practices · Crisis & risk management

Challenges vs Future Trends

Challenges: overtourism · environment · economic dependence · instability

Trends: smart destinations · regenerative · inclusive/accessible · slow tourism

flashcards.question: What is MASS TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
A QUANTITATIVE notion based on the proportion of the population participating in tourism or the volume of tourist activity (Burkart & Medlik, 1974).

It means 'extreme concentrations of tourists in one place, resulting in SATURATION'. It can't be tied to fixed numbers — every destination has a different CARRYING CAPACITY.

Origins: Thomas Cook's first organized group tour (1851); developed in Western societies from the 1950s.
flashcards.explanation: Mass tourism = volume + saturation relative to carrying capacity.

flashcards.question: What is FORDISM in tourism?
flashcards.answer:
A stage of 20th-century economic development = the system of MASS PRODUCTION (pioneered by Ford).

In tourism, Fordist systems secure ECONOMIES OF SCALE through large-scale, STANDARDISED and inflexible products — typified by low-cost INCLUSIVE PACKAGE HOLIDAYS from tour operators, who can dominate the distribution chain and depress prices paid to local hotels.
flashcards.explanation: Standardised package holidays = the Fordist model of tourism.

flashcards.question: What are LEAKAGES in tourism?
flashcards.answer:
The part of the price of the holiday paid by tourists that LEAVES or never reaches the destination, due to foreign-based transactions (Mitchell & Page, 2005; Meyer, 2006).

Example: eating at McDonald's, staying at a Hilton, or buying Coke — most of the money goes back to the origin country.
flashcards.explanation: Income that escapes the local economy.

flashcards.question: What is OVERTOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
Term coined by Skift (2016). 'The impact of tourism on a destination that EXCESSIVELY influences the perceived QUALITY OF LIFE of citizens and/or the quality of visitor experiences in a NEGATIVE way.'

It is a new buzzword for existing concepts of tourism CONGESTION MANAGEMENT and CARRYING CAPACITY (UNWTO 2019).
flashcards.explanation: The opposite of Responsible Tourism.

flashcards.question: What is Doxey's IRRIDEX, and what is 'tourismophobia'?
flashcards.answer:
Doxey's IRRITATION INDEX (Irridex, 1975) describes how residents' attitudes EVOLVE over time in response to tourism (from euphoria → apathy → irritation → antagonism).

TOURISMOPHOBIA ('turistofobia', Delgado 2008) describes the antagonistic relationship and escalating tensions between local hosts and incoming tourists (e.g. 'tourists go home' banners; Barcelona after the 1992 Olympics).
flashcards.explanation: Irridex tracks the escalation; tourismophobia is the extreme stage.

flashcards.question: What is CARRYING CAPACITY (UNWTO)?
flashcards.answer: "The maximum number of people that may visit a tourist destination at the same time, without causing destruction of the physical, economic and socio-cultural environment and an unacceptable decrease in the quality of visitors' satisfaction" (UNWTO, 2004).
flashcards.explanation: Key to managing congestion and overtourism.

flashcards.question: What is SPECIAL INTEREST TOURISM (SIT)?
flashcards.answer:
Tourism that occurs when the traveller's MOTIVATION and decision-making are primarily determined by a PARTICULAR SPECIAL INTEREST, with a focus on activity/ies and/or destinations/settings (Hall & Weiler, 1992).

Tourists seek emotional stimuli and experiences ('buy feelings, not products'). Often used as a synonym for NICHE tourism. It reflects the increasing diversity of interests of the late-modern leisure society.
flashcards.explanation: Interest/activity drives the decision — not the destination.

flashcards.question: What is the decision-making difference between GIT, MIT and SIT?
flashcards.answer:
• GIT (General Interest): 'WHERE would I like to go?' — destination first
• MIT (Mixed Interest): 'Where do I want to go AND what activities can I pursue there?'
• SIT (Special Interest): 'WHAT interest/activity do I want to pursue, and WHERE can I do it?' — interest first

For SITs, the destination is no longer primary — the interest/activity is.
flashcards.explanation: The shift from destination-led to interest-led decisions.

flashcards.question: How do General Interest vs Special Interest tourists differ?
flashcards.answer:
GENERAL INTEREST tourist: majority of travellers; lower/lower-middle income; price-sensitive; inexperienced; psychocentric; wants 'fashionable' destinations + high-quality accommodation.

SPECIAL INTEREST tourist: a MINORITY; middle/upper-middle income; LESS price-sensitive; experienced & sophisticated; allocentric/adventurous; high expectations of the activity (not necessarily accommodation); destinations are just contexts for the interest.
flashcards.explanation: Allocentric/experienced (SIT) vs psychocentric/price-sensitive (GIT).

flashcards.question: What are Cohen's 4 TOURIST ROLES (1972)?
flashcards.answer:
1. ORGANIZED MASS TOURIST — all-inclusive tour, 'environmental bubble', max familiarity
2. INDIVIDUAL MASS TOURIST — booked via operator but not bound to a group; slightly more novelty
3. EXPLORER — arranges own travel, avoids 'the beaten track', some familiarity (comfortable base)
4. DRIFTER — max novelty, immersed in local culture, shuns the tourist establishment
flashcards.explanation: From familiarity (mass) to novelty (drifter).

flashcards.question: What are the 4 levels of SIT participant intensity (Brotherton & Himmetoglu, 1997)?
flashcards.answer:
1. BEGINNERS — motivated to pursue a potential interest
2. ENTHUSIASTS — chose a fitting interest, know its boundaries
3. EXPERTS — selected and 'claimed' a special interest; wide knowledge
4. FANATICS — devoted to the field, described by others as 'crazy'
flashcards.explanation: Increasing depth of knowledge, skill and commitment.

learn.title: From Mass & Overtourism to Special Interest Tourism
learn.content:
Mass Tourism

Quantitative notion → volume + saturation vs carrying capacity
Origin: Thomas Cook (1851); boom from the 1950s
Fordism: standardised, inflexible, low-cost package holidays

The Problems

  • Leakages — money that escapes the local economy
  • Overtourism (Skift, 2016) — excessive negative impact on quality of life
  • Doxey's Irridex → 'tourismophobia' (e.g. Barcelona)
  • Carrying capacity — the max visitors without destruction/dissatisfaction

Special Interest Tourism (SIT)

Motivation driven by a particular special interest (≈ niche tourism). Decision logic: GIT 'where?' → MIT 'where + what?' → SIT 'what interest, then where?'

Typologies

Cohen (1972): organized mass → individual mass → explorer → drifter (familiarity → novelty)

Intensity: beginner → enthusiast → expert → fanatic

SIT tourist: minority, less price-sensitive, experienced, allocentric

flashcards.question: What is BUSINESS TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
A type of tourism activity in which visitors travel for a specific PROFESSIONAL and/or BUSINESS purpose to a place outside their workplace and residence, to attend a meeting, activity or event (UNWTO, 2019).

Key components: MEETINGS, INCENTIVES, CONFERENCES and EXHIBITIONS. It can be combined with other tourism types on the same trip.
flashcards.explanation: Travel for a professional/business purpose.

flashcards.question: What does MICE stand for, and what's the problem with the term?
flashcards.answer:
M = MEETINGS, I = INCENTIVES, C = CONFERENCES (or Congresses), E = EXHIBITIONS (or Events).

PROBLEM: there's no universally agreed definition, and almost no one outside the industry understands it — it's even criticised for its association with rodents/vermin. Alternatives: 'the meetings industry' (introduced 2006), 'business events' (Australia/Canada).
flashcards.explanation: MICE is catchy but poorly understood outside the trade.

flashcards.question: How does the SILK ROUTE relate to business travel history?
flashcards.answer:
In the Middle Ages the Silk Route was perhaps the greatest business travel route of all time. It was important in two ways:
1. It stimulated SUPPORT SYSTEMS for business travellers (accommodation/restaurants — the 'Caravanserai', camel traders, guides).
2. It moved IDEAS and INVENTIONS (gunpowder, astronomy, medicine) between Asia and Europe, and created major trading cities (e.g. Istanbul).
flashcards.explanation: Business travel is ancient — it began with trade.

flashcards.question: What are the main differences between LEISURE and BUSINESS tourism (demand side)?
flashcards.answer:
• WHO PAYS: leisure = the tourist; business = the employer/association (not the traveller)
• WHO DECIDES the destination: leisure = the tourist; business = the meeting/event organizer
• WHEN: leisure = holiday periods & weekends; business = all year, Mon–Fri (July/August avoided)
• DESTINATIONS: leisure = all kinds; business = mostly towns/cities in industrialized countries
flashcards.explanation: Different payer, decider, timing and destinations.

flashcards.question: Why is business tourism BENEFICIAL for destinations?
flashcards.answer:
• Tends to visit in OFF-PEAK season
• Relatively HIGH per-head per-day expenditure
• Business tourists are relatively WELL BEHAVED
• Brings business to many local suppliers (printers, florists, sign-makers…)
• Helps fund infrastructure (e.g. airports) and community leisure facilities
flashcards.explanation: High spend, off-peak, low impact — destinations love it.

flashcards.question: Distinguish CONFERENCE, CONVENTION and CONGRESS.
flashcards.answer:
• CONFERENCE — participatory meeting for discussion/problem-solving; no tradition/periodicity required; usually smaller scale, short duration
• CONVENTION — a general & formal meeting of a body/group to inform, deliberate or set policy; often with a secondary exhibition (US term for large national meetings)
• CONGRESS — regular coming-together of large groups, often several days with simultaneous sessions; (European term for convention)
flashcards.explanation: Scale & formality grow: conference < convention/congress.

flashcards.question: What is INCENTIVE TRAVEL?
flashcards.answer:
A motivational tool: participants receive a TRIP as a REWARD based on specific achievement levels set by management — mostly to increase sales.

Value for the company: bonding, reinforcing corporate culture, loyalty/retention, motivating non-winners. Value for participants: a more memorable prize than cash, networking, professional development, rest, 'trophy value'.
flashcards.explanation: A non-cash reward — often more effective than cash bonuses.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between a B2B and a B2C EXHIBITION?
flashcards.answer:
EXHIBITION = a temporary market event held regularly to showcase a sector and facilitate buying/selling ('shop window').

• TRADE SHOW / B2B — exhibitors from one industry; visitors buy for their business; often invitation/pre-registration; weekday; international/national reach
• CONSUMER SHOW / B2C — open to the public (entrance fee); sells directly to end-users; weekends; local/regional reach

(A 'mixed show' opens to trade then public, e.g. the Paris Air Show.)
flashcards.explanation: B2B = business buyers; B2C = the public.

flashcards.question: What are the ICCA vs UIA criteria for an international association meeting?
flashcards.answer:
ICCA (International Congress & Convention Association): organized by an international/regional association HQ; 50+ participants; held REGULARLY; rotates between at least 3 countries.

UIA (Union of International Associations): minimum 300 participants; lasting at least 3 days; representatives from at least 5 countries.
flashcards.explanation: ICCA = 50+/3 countries; UIA = 300+/3 days/5 countries.

learn.title: Business Tourism (MICE)
learn.content:
What is Business Tourism?

Travel for a professional/business purpose to attend an event.
MICE = Meetings · Incentives · Conferences · Exhibitions

Also called 'the meetings industry' (2006) or 'business events' — MICE is catchy but poorly understood outside the trade. Business travel is ancient (the Silk Route + Caravanserai).

Leisure vs Business (demand side)

Who pays? Employer/association · Who decides? The organizer · When? All year, Mon–Fri · Where? Cities in industrialized countries

Why Destinations Want It

Off-peak · high per-head spend · well-behaved · supports many local suppliers · funds infrastructure.

Key Formats

Conference < Convention/Congress (scale & formality)

Incentive travel — a trip as a reward (often beats cash)

Exhibitions: B2B (trade, weekday, invite) vs B2C (public, weekend, fee)

ICCA 50+/3 countries · UIA 300+/3 days/5 countries

flashcards.question: What is CULTURAL TOURISM (UNWTO, 2019)?
flashcards.answer:
A type of tourism where the visitor's essential motivation is to LEARN, DISCOVER, EXPERIENCE and CONSUME the tangible and intangible cultural attractions/products of a destination.

These relate to a society's material, intellectual, spiritual and emotional features: arts & architecture, historical/cultural heritage, culinary heritage, literature, music, creative industries and living cultures.
flashcards.explanation: Motivation = to learn/experience culture.

flashcards.question: What are the 3 areas included in cultural tourism (UNWTO, 2018)?
flashcards.answer:
1. TANGIBLE heritage — national/world heritage sites, monuments, historic buildings, cultural routes
2. INTANGIBLE heritage — crafts, gastronomy, festivals, music, oral traditions, religious/spiritual
3. CONTEMPORARY culture — film, performing arts, design, fashion, new media
flashcards.explanation: Tangible + intangible + contemporary.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between HERITAGE and HISTORY (and arts tourism)?
flashcards.answer:
HISTORY = the past itself.
HERITAGE = the modern-day USE and VALUATION of the past (for tourism, education, etc.) — 'what we inherit from the past and value in the present'.

Cultural tourism covers both HERITAGE tourism (artefacts of the past) and ARTS tourism (contemporary cultural production).
flashcards.explanation: Heritage = the present use of the past.

flashcards.question: What are McKercher's 5 TYPES of cultural tourist (2002)?
flashcards.answer:
Based on two dimensions — CENTRALITY (how important culture is to the trip) and DEPTH of experience:
1. PURPOSEFUL (high centrality / deep)
2. SIGHTSEEING (high centrality / shallow)
3. CASUAL (modest centrality / shallow)
4. INCIDENTAL (low centrality / shallow)
5. SERENDIPITOUS (low centrality / deep)
flashcards.explanation: Centrality × depth = 5 cultural-tourist types.

flashcards.question: What is the VALUE of tourism for culture, and of culture for tourism?
flashcards.answer:
VALUE OF TOURISM FOR CULTURE: generates resources for conservation, motivates communities to manage cultural assets, raises awareness of local heritage.

VALUE OF CULTURE FOR TOURISM: gives coherence to the destination offer, increases competitiveness, increases length of stay, spending and satisfaction.
flashcards.explanation: A two-way value relationship.

flashcards.question: What are the main TYPES of heritage attraction (Timothy, 2021)?
flashcards.answer:
• MUSEUMS (local, art, science, sports, music)
• HISTORIC THEME PARKS / folk-life museums (living museums, e.g. Plimoth Plantation)
• PERFORMING ARTS (opera houses, theatres — building + performance)
• ARCHAEOLOGICAL SITES & ancient monuments (Stonehenge, Pyramids, Acropolis)
• RELIGIOUS sites · LIVING culture / ethnic tourism · LITERARY & FILM locations
• AGRITOURISM & food tourism · SITES OF DEATH (dark tourism) · HERITAGE FESTIVALS
flashcards.explanation: A wide range — from museums to dark-tourism sites.

flashcards.question: What is the role of pilgrimage and the GRAND TOUR in heritage tourism history?
flashcards.answer:
PILGRIMAGE — one of the EARLIEST forms of heritage tourism: travel for spiritual/religious experiences to burial sites, miracle sites, healing places.

The GRAND TOUR (1600s–mid 1800s) — young European men of means travelled (with tutors) to classical art cities of Italy, France, etc. to become 'cultured nobility' — among the earliest prepackaged cultural tours.
flashcards.explanation: Pilgrimage + Grand Tour = historical roots of cultural tourism.

learn.title: Cultural Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Motivation = to learn, discover, experience and consume a destination's tangible & intangible cultural attractions (UNWTO, 2019).

Three Areas (UNWTO 2018)

  • Tangible — monuments, heritage sites, historic buildings
  • Intangible — crafts, gastronomy, festivals, music, oral/spiritual
  • Contemporary — film, performing arts, design, fashion, new media

Heritage vs History

History = the past. Heritage = the present-day use and valuation of the past. Cultural tourism = heritage tourism + arts tourism.

McKercher's 5 Cultural Tourists (centrality × depth)

Purposeful · Sightseeing · Casual · Incidental · Serendipitous

Heritage Attractions & History

Museums · living museums · performing arts · archaeological sites · religious sites · living culture · literary/film locations · agritourism · dark-tourism sites · festivals

Roots: pilgrimage (earliest) and the Grand Tour (1600s–1800s)

flashcards.question: What is INDUSTRIAL TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
A form of tourism that involves visits to modern WORK FACILITIES to view products and services, the PROCESS by which they are created, and the PEOPLE involved (Robinson, in Jafari 2003).

It is generally considered a form of CULTURAL TOURISM. Visits can be guided tours, observation from galleries, or purpose-built visitor centres (factories, mines, power plants, wineries, theatres).
flashcards.explanation: Visiting workplaces to see how things are made.

flashcards.question: What are the 2 TYPES of industrial tourism?
flashcards.answer:
1. ACTIVE industrial tourism — visits to WORKING companies/organisations, to learn about PRODUCTION PROCESSES in real time.

2. INDUSTRIAL HERITAGE tourism (industrial archaeology) — visits to INACTIVE / abandoned industrial sites, to learn about PAST industrial knowledge, culture and identity.
flashcards.explanation: Working sites (active) vs abandoned sites (heritage).

flashcards.question: What roles does industrial tourism play in ORGANISATIONS?
flashcards.answer:
• PUBLIC RELATIONS — building relations with the local community, employees, partners, media; improving reputation & corporate social responsibility; demonstrating 'green'/sustainable operations
• MARKETING — strengthening BRAND ATTACHMENT and encouraging purchases; factory tours & corporate museums as 'events & experiences' (Kotler & Keller)
flashcards.explanation: Two key business functions: PR and marketing.

flashcards.question: How does industrial tourism connect to the EXPERIENCE ECONOMY?
flashcards.answer:
In the experience economy, the economic value of an offering INCREASES from raw material → product → service → EXPERIENCE (Pine & Gilmore, 1998).

Experiences are built on four dimensions: ENTERTAINMENT, EDUCATIONAL, ESCAPIST and AESTHETIC. Industrial tourism turns work into a memorable, multi-sensory experience — and experiences are the foundation of special interest tourism.
flashcards.explanation: Work becomes a paid, memorable experience.

flashcards.question: What is the historical origin of industrial tourism?
flashcards.answer:
The first factory tours took place in GREAT BRITAIN in the 18th century. There is evidence tourists visited companies over 150 years ago — French vineyards & chocolate factories, US whiskey distilleries, tobacco factories, mines and stock exchanges.

MacCannell describes it as putting WORK ON DISPLAY — 'musealising' work and making it a tourist attraction.
flashcards.explanation: 18th-century Britain; 'work on display'.

flashcards.question: What does INDUSTRIAL HERITAGE protect, and why revitalise it?
flashcards.answer:
Industrial heritage = remains of TEXTILE, MINING, STEEL and similar heavy industries (TICCIH protects buildings, machinery, mills, mines, warehouses, power plants, transport, workers' social spaces).

Revitalising former industrial areas for tourism brings ECONOMIC (new jobs/income), SOCIAL (resident engagement) and CULTURAL (new identity, slowing depopulation) benefits — a sustainable way to divert crowds from saturated areas.
flashcards.explanation: Reusing the industrial past for regional renewal.

learn.title: Industrial Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Visits to work facilities to see products, the production process, and the people involved — generally a form of cultural tourism.

Two Types

Active — working companies, learn the production process in real time

Industrial heritage — abandoned/inactive sites (mines, mills), learn the past

Roles in Organisations

  • Public relations — reputation, community/employee/media relations, 'green' image
  • Marketing — brand attachment, encouraging purchases (factory tours, corporate museums)

Experience Economy

Value rises: raw material → product → service → experience (Pine & Gilmore). Four dimensions: entertainment, educational, escapist, aesthetic. Experiences are the foundation of special interest tourism.

History & Heritage

First factory tours: 18th-century Britain; 'work on display' (MacCannell). Industrial heritage (textile/mining/steel; protected by TICCIH) revitalises regions — economic, social & cultural renewal.

flashcards.question: What is NAUTICAL TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
A special form of tourism in which the tourist's main motivation is travel and stay ON or BY THE WATER using vessels (boats, yachts, cruise ships) for leisure, sport and recreation.

It combines navigation/sailing with the use of nautical infrastructure (marinas, ports) and coastal/maritime attractions. It is especially important for Croatia and the wider Mediterranean.

(Note: this category is based on general SIT knowledge — verify against the professor's slides.)
flashcards.explanation: Tourism centred on the water and vessels.

flashcards.question: What are the main SEGMENTS of nautical tourism?
flashcards.answer:
• CRUISING — large cruise-ship holidays (mass scale; e.g. Mediterranean/Caribbean itineraries)
• YACHTING / SAILING — private or chartered yachts and sailboats
• BOATING / CHARTER — renting vessels (bareboat or skippered)
• NAUTICAL infrastructure services — marinas, berths, repair/maintenance

Nautical tourism therefore ranges from mass (cruising) to clearly special-interest (sailing/yachting).
flashcards.explanation: Cruising, yachting/sailing, charter, marina services.

flashcards.question: What is a MARINA, and why is it the backbone of nautical tourism?
flashcards.answer:
A MARINA is a specially built port for nautical tourism — offering berths (moorings) plus services: water, electricity, fuel, repair, supply, sanitation, reception and hospitality.

Marinas are the basic infrastructure that makes yachting/charter tourism possible. In Croatia, the largest chain of marinas is ACI (Adriatic Croatia International Club).
flashcards.explanation: Marinas provide berths + services; ACI is Croatia's main chain.

flashcards.question: Why is CROATIA a leading nautical destination?
flashcards.answer:
• A long, indented Adriatic coastline with ~1,200 islands, islets and reefs
• Clean sea, many sheltered bays and short distances between ports
• A dense network of MARINAS (e.g. the ACI chain)
• Favourable sailing climate (good wind, long season)

Nautical tourism is one of the highest-yield, more sustainable forms of Croatian tourism.
flashcards.explanation: Indented coast + islands + marinas = ideal for sailing.

flashcards.question: What are the main CHARACTERISTICS of nautical tourism?
flashcards.answer:
• HIGH per-capita spending (yacht owners/charterers)
• Strong dependence on natural conditions (sea, coast, weather)
• Requires significant INFRASTRUCTURE investment (marinas, ports)
• Seasonal but can extend the season (off-peak sailing)
• Sensitive to environmental impacts (marine pollution, anchoring damage)
flashcards.explanation: High-spend, infrastructure-heavy, nature-dependent.

quiz.question: Nautical tourism is centred primarily on:
options: Travel and stay on or by the water using vessels

quiz.question: Which is a segment of nautical tourism?
A marina provides:
Croatia's largest chain of marinas is:
A key reason Croatia suits nautical tourism is its:
options: Indented coastline with many islands and sheltered bays

learn.title: Nautical Tourism
learn.content:
⚠️ The nautical lecture slide is image-only (no extractable text). This category is built from standard SIT knowledge — verify against the professor's slides.

What is Nautical Tourism?

Tourism centred on travel and stay on or by the water using vessels — combining sailing/navigation with marina infrastructure and coastal attractions.

Segments

  • Cruising — large cruise-ship holidays (mass scale)
  • Yachting / sailing — private or chartered yachts (special interest)
  • Charter / boating — renting vessels (bareboat or skippered)
  • Marina services — berths + water, fuel, repair, hospitality

Croatia

Indented Adriatic coast, ~1,200 islands, dense ACI marina network, good sailing climate → one of the highest-yield, more sustainable forms of Croatian tourism.

flashcards.question: What is SPORTS TOURISM (UNWTO, 2019)?
flashcards.answer:
"A type of tourism activity which refers to the travel experience of the tourist who either OBSERVES as a spectator or actively PARTICIPATES in a sporting event, generally involving commercial and non-commercial activities of a competitive nature."

Sport and tourism have been linked since ancient Greece and Rome (competitions motivated travel).
flashcards.explanation: Watching OR taking part in sport away from home.

flashcards.question: Tourism vs sport: what is the core difference (de Villiers)?
flashcards.answer:
TOURISM is an EXPERIENCE-orientated activity (it provides people with experiences).

SPORT is a PERFORMANCE-orientated activity (competitive; rewards grow with the level of competition).

The famous 'coffee' example (Pine) illustrates the experience economy: a coffee can be a product (1¢), commodity, service, or — in a trendy café — an EXPERIENCE (500¢).
flashcards.explanation: Experience-orientated (tourism) vs performance-orientated (sport).

flashcards.question: What is the difference between SPORTS TOURISM and TOURISM SPORT (Gammon & Robinson, 2003)?
flashcards.answer:
SPORTS TOURISM — SPORT is the PRIME motivation to travel (the tourism element reinforces it).

TOURISM SPORT — the HOLIDAY/visit is the prime motivation, and sport is a SECONDARY activity.

Each has a HARD definition (active/passive participation in COMPETITIVE sport) and a SOFT definition (recreational participation, e.g. skiing/walking holidays, or incidental sport).
flashcards.explanation: Which comes first — the sport or the holiday?

flashcards.question: What are Gibson's 3 categories of sport tourism (2002)?
flashcards.answer:
1. ACTIVE sport tourism — travelling to PARTICIPATE in sport
2. EVENT sport tourism — travelling to WATCH/attend a sporting event
3. NOSTALGIA sport tourism — visiting sport heritage (halls of fame, famous stadia, museums) — linked to worship, heritage, pilgrimage and fanship
flashcards.explanation: Active · event · nostalgia.

flashcards.question: What are Kurtzman's 5 SUPPLY-SIDE categories of sport tourism?
flashcards.answer:
1. ATTRACTIONS (stadiums, sport museums, halls of fame, sport theme parks)
2. RESORTS (sport as the primary focus, e.g. ski/golf resorts)
3. CRUISES (sport-focused cruises with pros on board)
4. TOURS (visiting multiple sport attractions/events)
5. EVENTS (sport events attracting spectator-tourists)
flashcards.explanation: Attractions, resorts, cruises, tours, events.

flashcards.question: How is DEMAND for tourism-sport classified (UNWTO, 7 groups)?
flashcards.answer:
By degree of involvement + importance of the tourism component:
1. Top-level athletes (the elite, <8% of athletes)
2. Second-level athletes
3. Youth groups
4. Sports enthusiasts & amateurs (the biggest group)
5. Tourists who want to practise sport when they travel
6. Tourists who practise sport casually
7. Spectators
flashcards.explanation: From elite athletes to casual spectators.

flashcards.question: How can MEGA EVENTS (Olympics, World Cup) benefit a host destination?
flashcards.answer:
• Re-brand / re-image a nation (Sydney 2000 accelerated awareness of Australia by ~10 years; Germany 'softened' its image with the 2006 FIFA World Cup)
• High media profile → world recognition; an agent of place-image change
• Long-term tourism boost after the event
• Benefits can be SPREAD beyond the host city (torch relay, training camps, cultural programmes, multiple venue cities)
flashcards.explanation: Mega events as nation-branding and 'fast-track' recognition.

quiz.question: In SPORTS TOURISM, the prime motivation to travel is:
Tourism is experience-orientated, whereas sport is:
Visiting a sports hall of fame or famous stadium is:
Which is one of Kurtzman's 5 supply-side categories of sport tourism?

fillBlanks.sentence: In sports tourism, _______ is the prime motivation to travel.
Tourism is experience-orientated; sport is _______-orientated.
Visiting sport heritage and halls of fame is _______ sport tourism.
The Olympics and World Cup can _______ a nation's image.
Top-level athletes represent less than _______% of all athletes.

learn.title: Sports Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Travel to observe (spectator) or actively participate in a sporting event (UNWTO, 2019). Tourism = experience-orientated; sport = performance-orientated.

Sports Tourism vs Tourism Sport (Gammon & Robinson)

Sports tourism: sport is the prime motivation

Tourism sport: the holiday is prime, sport is secondary

Each has a HARD (competitive) and SOFT (recreational/incidental) definition.

Gibson's 3 Categories

Active · Event · Nostalgia (sport heritage, halls of fame).

Kurtzman's 5 Supply-side Categories

Attractions · Resorts · Cruises · Tours · Events.

Demand (UNWTO, 7 groups)

Top-level athletes (<8%) · second-level · youth · enthusiasts/amateurs (biggest) · tourists who want to practise sport · casual · spectators.

Mega Events

Olympics/World Cup → nation re-branding (Sydney 2000, Germany 2006), world recognition, long-term tourism boost; spread benefits beyond the host city.

flashcards.question: What is LUXURY, and where does the word come from?
flashcards.answer:
Luxury is a MULTIFACETED concept — its definition depends on CONTEXT, GENERATION and NATIONALITY ('what one generation sees as a luxury, the next sees as a necessity').

The word derives from Latin 'LUX' / 'LUXURIA' = light, shine, excess, extravagance, deviation, lust.

Non-luxury and luxury are two extremes on a CONTINUUM — where ordinary ends and luxury begins is 'in the eyes of the beholder'.
flashcards.explanation: Context-dependent; from Latin lux/luxuria.

flashcards.question: What are MASSTIGE and the 'democratisation' of luxury?
flashcards.answer:
MASSTIGE = 'MASS' + 'preSTIGE'. A luxury brand REDUCES its price to become affordable to the masses, without compromising quality too much.

This 'democratisation' of luxury makes luxury reachable to many consumers regardless of income — but risks harming the traditional narrative meaning of luxury (which is based on RARITY).
flashcards.explanation: Mass prestige = accessible luxury for the masses.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between INACCESSIBLE and ACCESSIBLE luxury (Chang et al., 2016)?
flashcards.answer:
INACCESSIBLE luxury — the extreme level of authenticity, prestige, exclusivity, quality and innovativeness; sought by the UPPER socio-economic class (the traditional understanding of luxury).

ACCESSIBLE luxury — non-essential, prestigious, authentic products that are publicly well-known and REASONABLY PRICED; consumed by middle/working classes to express social status.
flashcards.explanation: Inaccessible (elite) vs accessible (reasonably priced).

flashcards.question: What are the 4 'lenses' for understanding luxury (Saviolo)?
flashcards.answer:
1. Luxury as a PRODUCT (durable investments vs personal goods; leather goods now dominate)
2. Luxury as a BUSINESS (4 elements: strong aspirational branding, superior quality + timelessness, high/premium pricing, aesthetics/design)
3. Luxury as a CULTURE (mainly European; France = 'art de vivre', heritage; Italy = excellence/innovation, 'la dolce vita')
4. Luxury as a CUSTOMER (heterogeneous; not all rich are luxury buyers; aspirational customers drive growth; Asia is booming)
flashcards.explanation: Product · Business · Culture · Customer.

flashcards.question: What is luxury NOT?
flashcards.answer:
• NOT just an object (it's objects + brands + business models + stories + service)
• NOT just expensive (it must give VALUE; high price signals quality but luxury ≠ expensive)
• NOT completely replicable (limited, made-to-measure, you wait — never a mass series)
• NOT easy (you need culture to understand it)
• NOT fast (true luxury needs TIME — unlike fashion)
flashcards.explanation: Defining luxury by what it is not.

flashcards.question: How do luxury SERVICES differ from luxury GOODS (Hemzo, 2023)?
flashcards.answer:
Luxury services share the general service characteristics — INTANGIBILITY, HETEROGENEITY, INSEPARABILITY, PERISHABILITY — plus:
• NON-OWNERSHIP (enjoyed for a limited time) but PSYCHOLOGICAL POSSESSION (valuable memories)
• LOWER conspicuous consumption (no visible logo)
• LOWER risk of counterfeiting (depend on savoir-faire/skills)

Managed with the 'service' 4 Ps: People, Processes, Panorama, Productivity.
flashcards.explanation: Services = experiences (intangible, non-owned, memory-based).

flashcards.question: What is BLUXURY, and what is the scale of luxury travel?
flashcards.answer:
BLUXURY = combining BUSINESS travel with LUXURY leisure travel (cf. 'bleisure' = business + leisure).

The luxury travel market is projected to reach ~USD $2.7 billion by 2032. Luxury travel is SUBJECTIVE and increasingly about acute PERSONALISATION; the 'hierarchy of luxury travel needs' applies Maslow's pyramid to travel.

The first 'boutique/designer hotel' was Morgans (New York, 1980s).
flashcards.explanation: Bluxury = business + luxury; market ~$2.7bn by 2032.

quiz.question: The word 'luxury' derives from the Latin:
'Masstige' means:
options: Maximum prestige for the elite only
Mass prestige — luxury made affordable to the masses

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the 4 'lenses' of luxury (Saviolo)?
According to the lecture, true luxury is:
'Bluxury' travel combines business travel with:
Inaccessible luxury is primarily sought by the:

fillBlanks.sentence: The word luxury comes from the Latin lux and _______.

learn.title: Luxury Tourism
learn.content:
What is Luxury?

Multifaceted, context/generation/nationality-dependent. From Latin lux/luxuria (light, excess). Non-luxury ↔ luxury = a continuum 'in the eyes of the beholder'.

Democratisation

Masstige (mass + prestige) makes luxury affordable to the masses, challenging luxury's traditional basis in rarity. Inaccessible (elite) vs accessible (reasonably priced) luxury.

4 Lenses (Saviolo)

Product · Business (branding, quality+timelessness, premium price, aesthetics) · Culture (France 'art de vivre' / Italy excellence) · Customer (heterogeneous; Asia booming)

Luxury is NOT

Not just an object · not just expensive · not replicable · not easy · not fast.

Luxury Travel

Services = experiences (intangible, non-owned, memory-based; 'service' 4 Ps: People, Processes, Panorama, Productivity). Bluxury = business + luxury. Market ~$2.7bn by 2032; first boutique hotel = Morgans, NYC.

flashcards.question: What is DARK TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
An UMBRELLA term for any form of tourism associated with DEATH, DISASTER and SUFFERING (Light, 2017).

The related niche term THANATOURISM (from Greek 'thanatos' = death) is more restrictive — it focuses on one's symbolic or actual encounter with death.

Examples: war memorials, holocaust museums, battlefields, concentration camps (many run by the public sector).
flashcards.explanation: Tourism linked to death, disaster and suffering.

flashcards.question: What is the central ETHICAL question of dark tourism?
flashcards.answer:
Where is the BOUNDARY between the ACCEPTABLE and UNACCEPTABLE transformation of suffering into a tourist attraction?

Dark tourism can be EDUCATIONAL and COMMEMORATIVE (ensuring suffering is not forgotten), but some visitors come for SENSATION / morbid curiosity / 'schadenfreude' — which can harm those emotionally affected. The right tone must be set, especially as many sites are publicly managed.
flashcards.explanation: Education/commemoration vs sensationalism/voyeurism.

flashcards.question: What are some early HISTORICAL precursors of dark tourism?
flashcards.answer:
Dark tourism is not new:
• Roman GLADIATORIAL games
• Public EXECUTIONS (medieval to 19th century) — with grandstands for fee-paying spectators
• The alleged first guided tour in England (1838) — a railway excursion to see a hanging
• Victorian MORGUE tours and flogging galleries
flashcards.explanation: Gladiators, public executions, morgue tours.

flashcards.question: What is Stone's DARK TOURISM SPECTRUM (2006)?
flashcards.answer:
A 'spectrum of supply' from the LIGHTEST to the DARKEST forms of dark tourism, based on spatial, temporal, political and ideological factors that determine the perceived intensity of 'darkness'.

It identifies SEVEN dark 'suppliers' / products from light → dark.
flashcards.explanation: A 'darkest–lightest' framework with 7 product types.

flashcards.question: What are Stone's 7 dark tourism 'suppliers' (light → dark)?
flashcards.answer:
1. DARK FUN FACTORIES — entertainment focus (e.g. the Dungeons; haunted houses)
2. DARK EXHIBITIONS — education/commemoration (e.g. WWII museums)
3. DARK DUNGEONS — former prisons/courthouses (Alcatraz, Clink Prison)
4. DARK RESTING PLACES — cemeteries (Père Lachaise, New Orleans)
5. DARK SHRINES — places of remembrance near the death (e.g. Queen Elizabeth II tributes; George Floyd Square)
6. DARK CONFLICT SITES — wars/battlefields (Normandy D-Day, the Alamo)
7. DARK CAMPS OF GENOCIDE — the darkest end (Auschwitz-Birkenau)
flashcards.explanation: Fun factories → exhibitions → dungeons → resting places → shrines → conflict → genocide.

flashcards.question: Compare ALCATRAZ and ROBBEN ISLAND as dark dungeons.
flashcards.answer:
Both are island prisons that held famous inmates, but their tourist interpretation differs greatly:
• ALCATRAZ (USA) — associated with ENTERTAINMENT (the 'Hollywood' image, famous criminals & escape attempts); visitors may pose for fun photos in cells.
• ROBBEN ISLAND (South Africa) — more EDUCATIONAL and CONTEMPLATIVE; guides are former apartheid-era prisoners; visitors come to learn about Nelson Mandela and South Africa's history.

Lesson: how a site is INTERPRETED shapes the visitor experience.
flashcards.explanation: Entertainment (Alcatraz) vs education/contemplation (Robben Island).

'Thanatourism' derives from the Greek word for:
Stone's dark tourism spectrum ranges from:
At the LIGHTEST (most entertainment-focused) end are:
Auschwitz-Birkenau is an example of:
options: A dark camp of genocide (the darkest end)

quiz.question: Compared with Alcatraz, Robben Island's tone is more:

fillBlanks.sentence: Dark tourism is associated with death, disaster and _______.
_______ (from Greek 'thanatos') focuses on the encounter with death.
Stone's spectrum runs from lightest to _______.
Dark fun _______ (e.g. the Dungeons) sit at the lightest end.
_______ is an example of the darkest end — a camp of genocide.

learn.title: Dark Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Umbrella term for tourism linked to death, disaster and suffering (Light, 2017).
Thanatourism (Greek 'thanatos' = death) = the encounter with death.

The Ethical Tension

Where is the boundary between acceptable (education/commemoration) and unacceptable (sensationalism, voyeurism, schadenfreude) use of suffering? Most sites are publicly managed and need a careful, respectful tone.

Stone's Dark Tourism Spectrum (2006) — 7 suppliers (light → dark)

1. Dark fun factories → 2. Dark exhibitions → 3. Dark dungeons → 4. Dark resting places → 5. Dark shrines → 6. Dark conflict sites → 7. Dark camps of genocide

Interpretation Matters

Alcatraz = entertainment/'Hollywood' image vs Robben Island = educational/contemplative (Mandela). How a site is interpreted shapes the experience.

flashcards.question: What is HEALTH TOURISM (UNWTO, 2019)?
flashcards.answer:
Tourism which has as a PRIMARY MOTIVATION the contribution to PHYSICAL, MENTAL and/or SPIRITUAL health through MEDICAL and WELLNESS-based activities that increase individuals' capacity to satisfy their needs and function better.

Health tourism is the UMBRELLA TERM for two subtypes: WELLNESS tourism and MEDICAL tourism.
flashcards.explanation: Umbrella term = wellness tourism + medical tourism.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between WELLNESS and MEDICAL tourism?
flashcards.answer:
WELLNESS tourism — tourist is 'WELL' but wants to improve; PREVENTIVE, PROACTIVE, voluntary, lifestyle-enhancing (fitness, healthy eating, relaxation, pampering). More pleasurable/fun.

MEDICAL tourism — tourist is usually ILL; uses EVIDENCE-BASED medical resources; mainly CURATIVE (diagnosis, treatment, cure, prevention, rehabilitation).

Henderson: travel for WELLNESS (beauty spas) vs travel for ILLNESS (medical interventions).
flashcards.explanation: Wellness = preventive (well); medical = curative (ill).

flashcards.question: Who is the 'father' of WELLNESS, and how did he define it?
flashcards.answer:
Halbert DUNN (1961). He described wellness as NOT merely the absence of disease, illness and stress, but the PRESENCE of:
• Purpose in life
• Active involvement in satisfying work and play
• Joyful relationships
• A healthy body and living environment
• Happiness
flashcards.explanation: Dunn: wellness = the PRESENCE of positives, not just absence of illness.

flashcards.question: What are the 3 sub-sets of WELLNESS tourism (UNWTO & ETC, 2018)?
flashcards.answer:
1. HOLISTIC — a whole/global approach to healing (body, mind, emotion, spirit); complementary/alternative therapies, acupuncture, naturopathy (often at purpose-built 'retreat centres')
2. SPIRITUAL — broader than religion; seeking higher consciousness/meaning (yoga, meditation, Tai Chi)
3. MEDICAL WELLNESS
flashcards.explanation: Holistic · spiritual · medical wellness.

flashcards.question: How do cultural understandings of health/wellness DIFFER by region (Smith & Puczkó)?
flashcards.answer:
• CENTRAL/EASTERN Europe & Baltics — physical/medical therapeutic healing (medicinal waters, muds, caves)
• SOUTHERN Europe — seaside wellness, thalassotherapy, Mediterranean diet, relaxed pace
• SCANDINAVIA — outdoor recreation, sauna (integral to everyday wellness)
• GERMANY/AUSTRIA/SWITZERLAND — fitness + healthy eating + spiritual (yoga, meditation)
• ASIA — yoga, meditation, energy flows (Reiki, Shiatsu, Feng Shui) integrated into daily life
flashcards.explanation: Health/wellness mean different things in different cultures.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between MEDICAL TOURISM and MEDICAL TRAVEL?
flashcards.answer:
MEDICAL TOURISM — a trip for medical treatment where the patient ALSO uses the destination's TOURIST infrastructure (sightseeing, shopping, cultural activities); recreational prospects in (often exotic) locations.

MEDICAL TRAVEL — travelling for the SOLE purpose of treatment; the traveller may NOT visit tourist attractions. Many authors argue 'medical travel' is the better term, as patients can only tour if well enough.
flashcards.explanation: Tourism (treatment + sightseeing) vs travel (treatment only).

flashcards.question: What FACTORS are shaping health tourism (UNWTO & ETC, 2018)?
flashcards.answer:
• More LEISURE TIME + disposable income for health/wellbeing
• Over-burdened HEALTH-CARE & insurance systems; rising long-term-care costs
• AGEING populations
• URBANISATION (over half the world lives in cities) → demand for escapism/natural alternatives
• LEGAL directives (e.g. EU Directive 2011/24 on cross-border health care)
• Global financial markets + investment; technology (m-health, wearables); data PRIVACY
• 'Reverse movement' of health travellers (developing → developed countries)
flashcards.explanation: Time/income, health-system strain, ageing, urbanisation, law, tech.

quiz.question: Health tourism is the umbrella term for:
Wellness tourism is mainly:
The 'father' of the wellness concept is:
Which is a sub-set of wellness tourism?
Travelling for the SOLE purpose of treatment (no sightseeing) is best called:
Which factor is shaping the growth of health tourism?
options: Ageing populations and over-burdened health systems

fillBlanks.sentence: Health tourism is the umbrella term for wellness tourism and _______ tourism.
Wellness tourism is mainly preventive, while medical tourism is mainly _______.
Halbert _______ is described as the father of the wellness concept.
Travelling solely for treatment, with no sightseeing, is medical _______.
Healing based on medicinal thermal water is called _______ (balneotherapy).

learn.title: Health Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Tourism whose primary motivation is physical, mental and/or spiritual health.
Umbrella term → WELLNESS tourism + MEDICAL tourism.

Wellness vs Medical

Wellness — tourist is 'well', wants to improve; preventive, proactive, fun

Medical — tourist is usually ill; evidence-based, curative

Dunn (1961): wellness = the presence of purpose, joy, health, happiness — not just absence of illness.

Wellness Sub-sets (UNWTO & ETC 2018)

Holistic · Spiritual · Medical wellness. Cultural understandings differ by region (CEE medicinal waters · Southern Europe thalassotherapy · Scandinavia sauna · Asia yoga/energy).

Medical Tourism vs Medical Travel

Tourism = treatment + use of tourist infrastructure; Travel = treatment only.

Factors Shaping It

Leisure time + income · strained health systems · ageing · urbanisation · EU cross-border directive · technology (m-health, wearables) · data privacy · 'reverse movement' of travellers.

flashcards.question: What is FILM TOURISM (Beeton, 2005)?
flashcards.answer:
Visitation to SITES where movies and TV programmes have been FILMED (and set), as well as tours to production studios, including film-related theme parks.

It is tourist activity induced by viewing a MOVING IMAGE — film, TV, pre-recorded products (DVD/Blu-Ray) and now digital media.
flashcards.explanation: Visiting filming locations, studios and film theme parks.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between FILM TOURISM and FILM-INDUCED TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
FILM TOURISM — visitation to a site associated with filming; the INCIDENTAL experience of tourists at film locations (they may not have been motivated by the film).

FILM-INDUCED TOURISM — tourism that is INFLUENCED/MOTIVATED by film or TV; it specifically MOTIVATES people to travel to a film location.

(The Eiffel Tower is 'film tourism' by definition even for visitors who never saw the films shot there.)
flashcards.explanation: Incidental (film tourism) vs motivated (film-induced).

flashcards.question: How are films 'PULL' factors in 'PUSH' locations?
flashcards.answer:
In tourist motivation theory, PULL factors attract the tourist to a destination, while PUSH factors predispose a person to travel.

Movies make destination attractions into PULL factors that are situated in the tourist-GENERATING ('push') location — i.e. the attraction is experienced VICARIOUSLY at home (cinema), with longer exposure than ads and no 'hard sell'.
flashcards.explanation: Films bring the destination's pull to the viewer's home.

flashcards.question: What are Macionis's 3 types of film tourist (2004)?
flashcards.answer:
By level of interest in film:
1. SPECIFIC film tourist — actively seeks out places seen in film (highest interest)
2. GENERAL film tourist — not specifically drawn to a location but joins film-tourism activities while there (moderate)
3. SERENDIPITOUS film tourist — just happens to be at a destination portrayed in a film (lowest)

(Connell & Meyer added the 'ELITE film tourist' — visiting purely to view the location, no other motive.)
flashcards.explanation: Specific → general → serendipitous (+ elite).

flashcards.question: Are most film-site visitors SPECIAL INTEREST film tourists?
flashcards.answer:
NO — in short, NOT MANY. Most are casual/incidental/serendipitous.

Evidence: only 0.3% deemed Lord of the Rings the MAIN reason for visiting New Zealand (+9% one of several reasons); ~one-third of LOTR-tour participants had NEVER watched the film. Visitors are mostly drawn by the LANDSCAPE/scenery the film revealed, rather than the film itself (86% cited scenery for NZ).
flashcards.explanation: The scenery (not the film per se) usually drives the visit.

flashcards.question: What does the DUBROVNIK / GAME OF THRONES case show?
flashcards.answer:
HBO moved King's Landing filming to Dubrovnik (from Season 1, 2011); the Croatian DMO marketed Dubrovnik as a synonym for King's Landing.

Result (Tkalec et al., 2017): Game of Thrones film-induced tourism produced a ~37.9% increase in tourist arrivals, ~28.5% more overnight stays, and ~37.5% more City Walls tickets — far above the pre-GoT period. Depken et al.: ~59,000 additional overnights per year, with a STRONGER effect in the OFF-SEASON.
flashcards.explanation: Croatia's flagship film-induced tourism success.

flashcards.question: What are the POSITIVE and NEGATIVE impacts of film tourism on a destination?
flashcards.answer:
POSITIVE: more tourists → more revenue & employment; infrastructure improvement; product diversification; cultural exchange; can fund HERITAGE preservation (admission fees).

NEGATIVE: conflict, COMMODITIZATION, loss of AUTHENTICITY, exploitation of natural/cultural environment; films can also project NEGATIVE images/stereotypes of a destination (e.g. drugs, crime). DMOs cannot control media representations.
flashcards.explanation: Revenue & heritage funding vs commoditization & stereotypes.

learn.title: Film Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Visitation to filming sites, studios and film theme parks (Beeton, 2005) — tourist activity induced by a moving image (film, TV, digital).

Film vs Film-induced

Film tourism = incidental visitation to film sites

Film-induced tourism = travel specifically motivated by the film

Films = pull factors situated in push (home) locations.

Types of Film Tourist

Macionis: specific → general → serendipitous (+ Connell & Meyer's 'elite'). Most visitors are NOT special-interest film tourists — they're drawn by the scenery the film revealed.

Dubrovnik & Game of Thrones

King's Landing filmed in Dubrovnik (2011) → ~37.9% more arrivals, ~37.5% more City Walls tickets (Tkalec et al.); ~59,000 extra overnights/year, stronger in the OFF-season.

Impacts

+ revenue, jobs, infrastructure, heritage funding · − commoditization, loss of authenticity, negative stereotypes (DMOs can't control media).

flashcards.question: Which topics make up the two midterm 'halves' that the final combines?
flashcards.answer:
1st midterm (lectures 1–6): Introduction to tourism, Destination management, From mass/over-tourism to SIT, Business tourism, Cultural tourism, Industrial tourism.

2nd midterm (lectures 8–15): Nautical, Sports, Luxury, Dark, Health and Film tourism.
flashcards.explanation: K1 = foundations + first types; K2 = the specialised SIT types.

flashcards.question: EXAM REVIEW: What is SPECIAL INTEREST TOURISM, and how does its decision logic differ from GIT?
flashcards.answer:
SIT = tourism where the traveller's motivation is determined by a PARTICULAR SPECIAL INTEREST (≈ niche tourism).

Decision logic: GIT asks 'WHERE shall I go?' (destination-led); SIT asks 'WHAT interest do I want to pursue, and where can I do it?' (interest-led). SIT tourists are a minority — experienced, less price-sensitive, allocentric.
flashcards.explanation: The interest, not the destination, drives the SIT decision.

flashcards.question: Cross-topic: which SIT types are sub-forms of CULTURAL tourism?
flashcards.answer:
• INDUSTRIAL tourism is generally considered a form of CULTURAL tourism.
• DARK tourism overlaps with cultural/heritage tourism (sites of death & suffering).
• FILM tourism emerged as a niche of cultural tourism (alongside heritage, arts, gastronomic, creative).

Cultural tourism itself = tangible + intangible + contemporary culture (UNWTO 2018).
flashcards.explanation: Cultural tourism is the broad umbrella for several SIT types.

flashcards.question: Cross-topic: how does the EXPERIENCE ECONOMY (Pine & Gilmore) appear across SIT?
flashcards.answer:
Value rises: raw material → product → service → EXPERIENCE.

• INDUSTRIAL tourism turns work into a memorable multi-sensory experience.
• SPORTS tourism: tourism is 'experience-orientated' (the coffee example: a $5 Starbucks coffee = an experience).
• LUXURY tourism: luxury services are experiences (intangible, non-owned, memory-based).

Experiences are the foundation of special interest tourism.
flashcards.explanation: The experience economy underpins SIT broadly.

flashcards.question: EXAM REVIEW: Match the typology to its author — cultural tourists, tourist roles, film tourists, dark tourism spectrum.
flashcards.answer:
• McKERCHER (2002) — 5 CULTURAL tourists (centrality × depth): purposeful/sightseeing/casual/incidental/serendipitous
• COHEN (1972) — 4 TOURIST roles: organized mass / individual mass / explorer / drifter
• MACIONIS (2004) — 3 FILM tourists: specific / general / serendipitous (+ elite)
• STONE (2006) — DARK tourism spectrum: 7 suppliers, lightest → darkest
flashcards.explanation: Four key typologies and their authors.

flashcards.question: Cross-topic: how does CROATIA feature across SIT types?
flashcards.answer:
• NAUTICAL — indented Adriatic coast + ~1,200 islands + ACI marinas → a leading nautical destination
• MASS/OVERTOURISM — pronounced seasonality; 92.5% of accommodation on the coast
• FILM — Dubrovnik as 'King's Landing' (Game of Thrones) → ~37.9% more arrivals
• CULTURAL — Dubrovnik Old Town (UNESCO World Heritage); Croatian National Theatre
flashcards.explanation: Croatia recurs as a case study across the course.

learn.title: Final Exam Practice — How to Use
learn.content:
What is this category?

A cross-topic practice set combining all course topics — exactly how the final mixes them. Use it AFTER reviewing the two midterm halves.

The course in one map

FOUNDATIONS (1–3): tourism definitions & SDGs · destination management · mass/over-tourism → SIT
K1 TYPES (4–6): business (MICE) · cultural · industrial
K2 TYPES (8–15): nautical · sports · luxury · dark · health · film

Cross-topic favourites

  • GIT vs MIT vs SIT decision logic; the SIT tourist profile
  • Typologies: McKercher (cultural) · Cohen (roles) · Macionis (film) · Stone (dark spectrum)
  • Cultural tourism as the umbrella for industrial / dark / film
  • Experience economy across industrial, sports and luxury
  • Health tourism = wellness (preventive) + medical (curative)
  • Croatia case studies: nautical (ACI), Dubrovnik (GoT), overtourism seasonality
